A running log of past sessions and their outcomes, so Claude can pick up where the last one ended
questions.explanation: CLAUDE.md is standing project memory: short, high-value instructions loaded into every session. Long documents cost context on every task and are better read on demand; secrets do not belong in a checked-in file; session history is what memory files or notes are for.

questions.question: A team wants every file Claude Code edits to be run through the formatter, without relying on the model to remember. Which mechanism is right?
options: A CLAUDE.md instruction asking Claude to run the formatter after each edit it makes
A PostToolUse hook matched to the edit tools that runs the formatter on the changed file
A custom slash command that formats the tree, which the developer runs at the end of a session
A formatting subagent that the main session delegates to once the edits are complete
questions.explanation: Hooks are deterministic shell steps tied to tool events; they run whether or not the model remembers. A CLAUDE.md note is advisory, and a slash command or subagent still depends on someone invoking it.

questions.question: How would you run Claude Code non-interactively inside a CI job?
options: Print mode with the -p flag, passing the prompt and a restricted allowed-tools list
An interactive session on the runner with the permission mode set to accept every action
A plan-mode session, since planning does not edit files and so needs no approvals
A subagent launched from a developer's local session, with the CI job waiting on its result
questions.explanation: Print mode runs a single prompt headlessly and exits, and restricting tools keeps a CI run from taking actions nobody reviewed. An interactive session with accept-all permissions has no human present and no bound on what runs.

questions.question: A session has been running for hours and answers are getting worse and slower. What is the first thing to try?
options: Switch the session to a larger model so it can hold more of the accumulated conversation
Disable hooks for the rest of the session, since each hook adds latency to every tool call
Paste the full transcript so far back in as a new user message so nothing is lost
Compact or clear the context, then re-brief the task with only what the next step needs
questions.explanation: Quality degrades as the window fills with stale material; compaction and clearing exist to fight exactly this. Pasting the transcript back doubles the bulk that caused the problem, and a larger model does not shrink the window's contents.

questions.question: You need a response in a strict JSON shape that downstream code will parse. Which approach is most reliable?
options: Ask for JSON in the user message and add a note that any text outside the object will break the parser
Define the shape as a tool input schema, or use structured outputs, so the model must conform
Lower the temperature to zero so the formatting is deterministic across runs
Prefill the assistant turn with an opening brace and stop at the closing brace
questions.explanation: Schema-enforced output is more reliable than instructions alone: tool use with an input schema, or structured outputs, constrains the shape. Prefilling the brace suppresses preamble but does not guarantee the keys, types, or nesting downstream code expects.

questions.question: A prompt includes a 40-page contract and one question about it. Where should the question go?
options: At the top of the user message, before the contract, so the model knows what to look for while it reads
In the system prompt, with the contract alone in the user turn, so instruction and content are separated
At the end of the user message, after the contract, with the contract clearly delimited by tags
Split across several user turns, one section of the contract per turn, with the question at the end
questions.explanation: For long context, put documents first and the question last, and delimit the document so instructions and content do not blur. Putting the question first is the common intuition but performs worse on long inputs; moving it to the system prompt separates it from the material it refers to.

questions.question: Output format keeps drifting despite detailed instructions. What usually fixes it fastest?
options: Restate the format instruction at both the start and the end of the prompt so it is harder for the model to miss
Remove the system prompt and put the instructions in the user turn, closer to the task
Reduce max_tokens so the model has no room to add anything beyond the required format
Add two or three high-quality examples of the exact format, wrapped in clearly labeled tags
questions.explanation: A small number of good examples steers format more reliably than longer descriptions. Repeating the instruction adds emphasis, not clarity; cutting max_tokens truncates output rather than shaping it.

questions.question: When is extended thinking the wrong tool?
options: A high-volume yes/no classifier where per-request cost and latency dominate
Multi-step planning over a set of requirements that conflict with one another
Debugging a subtle logic error across several interacting functions
Weighing the trade-offs between two candidate system architectures
questions.explanation: Extended thinking costs tokens and time. It pays off on hard reasoning such as planning, debugging, and trade-off analysis, not on simple, high-volume decisions where a fast direct answer is just as accurate.

questions.question: A tool named q with the description "queries db" is being called at the wrong times with the wrong arguments. Best fix?
options: Add separate tools for each common query so the model no longer has to work out the arguments
Add a system prompt rule that the model should think carefully before every database query
Rename it and write a description covering when to use it, what each parameter means, and edge cases
Return a longer error message from the tool whenever the arguments do not match a known query
questions.explanation: The description is what the model reads to decide when and how to call a tool; write it for the model, with parameter meanings, edge cases, and an example. More tools with the same thin descriptions multiply the confusion, and error messages only help after a wrong call has already been made.

questions.question: You need the model to call one specific tool on this turn, no matter what. Which setting?
options: tool_choice set to any, so the model must call some tool
tool_choice set to that tool by name, forcing the call
tool_choice set to auto with the tool listed first in tools
disable_parallel_tool_use set to true and one tool listed
questions.explanation: tool_choice with a specific tool name forces that call. any forces some tool but leaves the choice to the model; auto leaves the decision to the model entirely, regardless of tool order; disable_parallel_tool_use limits how many calls happen, not whether one does.

questions.question: An MCP server will run on the developer's own machine, launched by the client as a child process. Which transport?
options: Streamable HTTP on localhost
WebSockets over a public URL
Server-sent events endpoint
stdio over the child process
questions.explanation: stdio is the transport for a local server the client launches as a child process. Streamable HTTP is for remote servers that many clients connect to; running it on localhost works but adds a network layer and a port for no benefit here.

questions.question: A tool call fails because the record does not exist. What should the tool return so the agent can recover?
options: A tool result flagged as an error, with a message saying the record was not found and what ids are valid
A successful empty result, so the loop continues and the model infers the record was missing
The raw exception and stack trace from the database driver, so the model can see exactly which query failed
No result for that call, holding the turn until a person can look up the record by hand
questions.explanation: Error results with actionable messages let the model choose a different path. An empty success hides the failure and invites the model to proceed on a missing record; a raw stack trace is an error the model has to decode rather than act on.

questions.question: You want prompt caching to work across many requests that share a large system prompt and tool set. How should the prompt be ordered?
options: Volatile user content first, then the system prompt and tool definitions, with a cache breakpoint at the very end
Stable content first (system prompt, tool definitions), a cache breakpoint after it, volatile content last
Everything inside one user message in a fixed order, so the whole request is cached as one block
Tools first, then the user content, then the system prompt, with a breakpoint after each section
questions.explanation: Caching matches prefixes. Stable material goes first so the cached prefix is reused; anything that changes per request goes after it. A breakpoint at the very end after volatile content caches a prefix that no other request will match.

questions.question: A coordinator delegates research to a subagent. What should the coordinator pass, and what should it get back?
options: The whole conversation so far, and the subagent's complete transcript back, so nothing is lost
A pointer to the coordinator's memory file, and the subagent's full transcript back for review
A complete, self-contained brief with everything the subagent needs, and only the conclusion back
A one-line task title, since the subagent shares the coordinator's context and can look up the rest
questions.explanation: Subagents start with a clean context. Give them a complete brief and take back the result, not the working, to keep the coordinator's window lean. Passing the whole conversation both ways defeats the purpose of delegation; a pointer to a memory file leaves the subagent without the task.

questions.question: A document pipeline runs the same three steps on every input: extract entities, normalize them, then write a summary. Each step's output feeds the next. Which pattern is this?
options: Orchestrator-workers, with a planner assigning steps
Parallelization, with the three steps run at once
Evaluator-optimizer over the summary step
Prompt chaining, with each output feeding the next
questions.explanation: Fixed sequential steps where each output feeds the next is prompt chaining. Parallelization does not fit because normalize depends on extract; an orchestrator adds planning cost and nondeterminism to a path that never changes.

questions.question: Three independent checks (toxicity, PII, and policy) must run on every response before it is shown. Latency matters. Which pattern?
options: Run the three checks concurrently and aggregate the verdicts
Chain the checks in sequence so each one sees the previous verdict
Have one classifier call decide which checks are needed
Fold all three checks into a single call with one prompt
questions.explanation: Independent work with no dependencies is the parallelization pattern; running the checks concurrently cuts latency. Folding them into one call is tempting but mixes three jobs in one prompt and makes each verdict harder to test on its own.

questions.question: When does Anthropic's guidance say to reach for an agent instead of a workflow?
options: When the task is large enough that a single prompt cannot hold all of the input
When the steps are known in advance but each step needs a different model
When the number of steps cannot be predicted and the model must choose its path from results
When latency is not a concern and the budget comfortably allows several model calls for each request
questions.explanation: Agents earn their cost when the path is open-ended and the model must decide the next step from what it finds. Known steps with different models is a workflow with per-step model choice; a large input calls for retrieval or chunking, not autonomy.

questions.question: An agent for booking travel has succeeded in demos but sometimes loops forever in production. The most important missing control is:
options: A more detailed persona and goal statement so the agent stays focused on the booking
A maximum turn count and a stop condition the loop checks on every iteration
A larger context window so earlier attempts remain visible and are not repeated
A wider tool set so the agent has an alternative route when one provider fails
questions.explanation: Every agent loop needs an explicit termination condition and a hard cap on turns, or a confused model runs up the bill. A larger window makes the loop remember more but does not end it; more tools give it more ways to keep going.

questions.question: Which is the strongest reason to start a new client project with workflows rather than agents?
options: Workflows can be built without prompt engineering, so the client's own team can maintain them
Agents require the Agent SDK, which most client environments cannot run
Workflows are what stakeholders expect and are easier to present in a demo
Workflows are predictable, testable, and cheaper, building the trust needed before autonomy
questions.explanation: Predictability and testability come first. Autonomy is added where the evidence says it pays. Workflows still contain prompts, so maintainability without prompt work is not the argument, and the API supports agents without any special runtime.

questions.question: An orchestrator delegates research to three subagents and then writes a report. One subagent returns nothing useful. What should the design do?
options: Detect the gap, retry or re-scope the subtask, and proceed with what it has when retries run out
Fail the whole run and surface the empty result, since a partial report could mislead whoever reads it
Drop that topic from the report and note in the log that the subagent returned no content
Hand the empty topic back to the user with a question about whether the report should continue
questions.explanation: Robust orchestration treats subagent failure as a normal event with a recovery path and a bounded retry budget. Failing the whole run throws away two good results for one bad one; dropping the topic silently hides the gap from the reader.

questions.question: A coding agent must never run a destructive git command. Which enforcement is reliable?
options: A system prompt rule listing every destructive git command the agent must not run
A CLAUDE.md section describing which git operations are off limits in this repo
A PreToolUse hook or permission rule that blocks matching commands before they execute
A lower temperature setting so the agent sticks to the conservative commands it has already seen
questions.explanation: Deterministic gates outside the model are the reliable layer. Prompts and CLAUDE.md are advisory: they lower the odds of a bad call but cannot block one, and temperature changes sampling, not policy.

questions.question: You are asked to justify why an agent design uses a single coordinator instead of a swarm of peer agents that message each other freely. The best justification:
options: Peer agents cannot share tool results, so a coordinator is needed to relay them
A coordinator keeps control flow observable and debuggable, and bounds each subagent's context
Peer messaging is slower in practice because every message needs its own model call
The API's multi-agent support is built around a single coordinator, so peer swarms need extra scaffolding
questions.explanation: Hub-and-spoke designs are easier to trace, test, and constrain than free-form peer messaging. The speed argument is not reliable, since a coordinator also spends calls; the API does not mandate either topology.

questions.question: A customer wants an agent that autonomously sends emails on their behalf. What belongs in the first release?
options: Autonomous sending for all emails except the ones the model itself flags as sensitive
Full autonomy from day one, with a daily audit of what was sent so problems are caught early
Autonomous sending for internal recipients only, expanding to external once a week has passed
Draft-then-approve: the agent prepares emails and a person sends, with autonomy earned on measured accuracy
questions.explanation: Outbound actions with reputational risk start behind a human gate; autonomy expands as evidence accumulates. Letting the model flag its own sensitive cases makes the model the gate it is supposed to be behind; a daily audit catches problems after the email has gone out.

questions.question: Which metric best tells you an agent is worth its cost in production?
options: Task completion rate at acceptable quality, measured per dollar and per minute
Average tokens consumed per completed task, trended week over week
Share of runs that finish without any tool errors or retries
Number of tasks handled per day compared with what the human team handled before
questions.explanation: Outcome per cost is the measure. Tokens per task is an input, not value; runs without tool errors can still produce wrong answers; tasks per day ignores quality and cost.

questions.question: An evaluator-optimizer loop keeps running for many iterations without converging. What is the likely design flaw?
options: The generator runs at too high a temperature, so each draft moves in a new direction
The evaluator and generator share a prompt, so the judge is biased toward its own output
The evaluator's criteria are vague, so 'good enough' is never reached; it needs pass criteria and a round cap
The loop has no memory of earlier drafts, so it keeps repeating the same corrections
questions.explanation: Refinement loops need crisp acceptance criteria and a maximum number of rounds. Temperature and draft memory can add noise, but a loop with a clear pass condition and a cap terminates regardless; without them, no tuning of the generator helps.

questions.question: A routing workflow classifies requests into billing, technical, and sales. Ten percent of requests fit none. What should the design include?
options: Retry classification with a second model until every request lands in one of the three
A fallback route for 'other' that goes to a general handler or to a person
A confidence threshold that forces low-confidence requests into the nearest bucket
A fourth category learned from the unclassified requests after launch
questions.explanation: Routers need an explicit fallback path; forcing fits produces confident wrong handling. Retrying with another model still forces a fit, and a nearest-bucket threshold is the same forced fit with a number attached.

questions.question: Which statement about tools in agent loops is correct?
options: Tool results should be passed back as a user turn so that the model treats them as fresh instructions to follow
Tool results can only carry text, so binary or structured data must be described in the prompt
Tools must be called in the order they are listed, so ordering in the tools array matters
Tool results are data the model reasons over; instructions come from the system prompt and user
questions.explanation: Treating tool output as data rather than instructions is the basis of injection resistance and clean reasoning. Tool results do travel in a user turn as tool_result blocks, but that is a transport detail; it does not make them instructions.

questions.question: A team wants to run twenty subagents in parallel for a research task. What should they watch first?
options: That each subagent has a complete, self-contained brief and a bounded budget
That all subagents share one context window so they do not duplicate work
That every subagent uses the same tool set so the results have a common shape
That the coordinator holds no context of its own and only merges the results
questions.explanation: Parallel fan-out multiplies whatever you give it. Clear briefs and budgets per worker keep it useful. A shared window is not how subagents work and would defeat the isolation; identical tool sets do not make briefs clearer.

questions.question: An agent must decide between continuing a task and asking the user a question. Good design says it should ask when:
options: It has consumed half of its token budget for the task at hand
Any tool call in the current step has returned an error
The next action is irreversible, ambiguous, or outside its granted scope
It has finished one subtask and the next one on the list belongs to a different owner
questions.explanation: Human checkpoints belong at irreversible or ambiguous decisions, not at arbitrary points. A tool error is usually something the loop should handle with a retry or an alternate path; a token milestone says nothing about risk.

questions.question: A workflow uses one large model call to do classification, extraction, and a summary at once, and quality is uneven. What is the usual improvement?
options: Switch to a larger model so it can handle the three tasks in one pass
Decompose into chained steps so each call has one job and can be checked
Enable extended thinking so the model plans all three outputs before writing
Drop the summary from the call and generate it separately with a template
questions.explanation: Splitting a multi-task prompt into single-purpose steps improves accuracy and makes each step testable. Extended thinking helps hard reasoning but does not fix a prompt that mixes three jobs; dropping one task is only a partial decomposition.

questions.question: What is the practical reason to log every tool call, its inputs, and its result in an agent system?
options: Compliance reporting, since most regulated industries require a record of automated actions
Cost control, since tool call logs are the only way to reconstruct token usage per task
Prompt caching, since logged calls can be replayed as a cached prefix on the next run
Debugging, evaluation, and audit: you cannot improve or explain behavior you did not record
questions.explanation: Observability is how agent behavior is understood, evaluated, and defended. Compliance is one use, not the practical reason; usage is reported per request by the API, and logs have nothing to do with cache prefixes.

questions.question: A client says 'make it fully autonomous' for an agent that changes production database records. Your recommendation as the architect:
options: Autonomy for reads and reversible changes, approval for irreversible ones, with an audit trail, revisited as data comes in
Full autonomy as requested, with a nightly database backup so any bad change can be restored
Full autonomy with logging turned off in the hot path so approval latency does not slow the agent
Read-only access for the agent, with all writes handled by a separate scheduled job the client owns
questions.explanation: Blast radius sets the gate. Irreversible actions get approval until evidence justifies more. A nightly backup limits damage after the fact but does not prevent a customer-visible change; read-only for everything gives up the value the client asked for.

questions.question: A developer complains Claude Code re-explores the codebase every session. The cheapest fix is:
options: A longer first prompt each session that walks through the directory layout
A CLAUDE.md with the project's structure, commands, and conventions
A subagent that explores the codebase and reports back at the start of each session
A memory file the developer pastes into the first message of every session
questions.explanation: CLAUDE.md is loaded automatically and is the place for standing project knowledge. An exploring subagent still spends the exploration every session; a pasted file is CLAUDE.md done by hand.

questions.question: You want Claude Code to plan before it edits on a large refactor. Which feature matches?
options: A PreToolUse hook that rejects edit calls until a plan file exists in the repository
Headless mode with a prompt asking for a written plan and no tool access
Plan mode, which explores and proposes an approach before any file changes
A custom slash command that runs the test suite before each edit is applied
questions.explanation: Plan mode separates thinking from editing so you can review the approach first. A hook that blocks edits enforces a gate but gives you no plan to review; headless mode is for automation, not a review step.

questions.question: A repeated workflow, 'update the changelog from recent commits', should be one command. Which Claude Code feature?
options: A custom slash command or skill that captures the prompt and steps
A PostToolUse hook on git commit that appends the message to the changelog
A subagent dedicated to changelog work, invoked from the main session
An MCP server exposing a changelog tool that reads the git history
questions.explanation: Reusable prompts belong in slash commands or skills; hooks are for deterministic shell steps. A hook on commit fires per commit and cannot write a summarized changelog on demand; an MCP server adds a tool, not a reusable workflow.

questions.question: Which permission approach is right for a shared CI runner using Claude Code?
options: Accept every tool call automatically, since no developer is present to approve
Prompt the developer who pushed the commit for each tool approval via chat
Deny every tool so the run is a pure text response with no side effects
An explicit allow list of tools and commands, with no interactive approvals
questions.explanation: Headless runs cannot ask a human, so the allowed surface is defined up front and kept narrow. Accepting everything removes the boundary; denying every tool leaves Claude unable to read the code it is meant to work on.

questions.question: Where does an MCP server configuration belong when it should apply to everyone working in the repository?
options: In each developer's user-level settings, synced through a dotfiles repository
In the system prompt for the session, listed as servers Claude should connect to
In the project-scoped configuration checked into the repository
In a SessionStart hook that registers the servers when Claude Code launches
questions.explanation: Project scope travels with the repo; user scope is personal. A dotfiles sync approximates it but relies on every developer keeping up; the system prompt cannot register a server.

questions.question: A hook that blocks a tool call should communicate the reason. Why?
options: So the model can adjust its plan instead of retrying the same blocked action
So the block is written into the transcript for the developer to review later on
So the hook's exit code can be mapped to the right billing category
So the model can override the block when the reason does not apply
questions.explanation: Feedback from a blocked call lets the model take a different path. Logging is a side benefit, not the point; a hook's reason is information for the model, not a mechanism to override the block.

questions.question: Which task is a good fit for a Claude Code subagent?
options: Reading CLAUDE.md at the start of a session and summarizing its rules back to the user
A large, self-contained investigation whose details would clutter the main session
Applying a one-line change that the main session has already located
Changing the permission settings so the main session can run a tool
questions.explanation: Subagents isolate context. Delegate work whose transcript you do not need in the main thread. A one-line change is cheaper to make directly, and CLAUDE.md is already loaded for the main session.

questions.question: A team notices Claude Code sometimes runs the test suite three times in a row. Which is the right lever?
options: A stricter system prompt telling Claude to run the tests only once per task
Removing the test command from the allowed tools and running tests in CI instead
Increasing the max turns so the session can finish before the loop is cut off
A hook or CLAUDE.md rule defining when tests run, plus a check of the loop for missing stop conditions
questions.explanation: Repeated actions point to missing structure: explicit rules for when to run tests and clear stop conditions. Removing the command hides the symptom and slows feedback; more turns give the loop more room to repeat.

questions.question: What does the /compact style operation do in a long session?
options: Summarizes the conversation so far to free context while keeping the essentials
Trims tool results from the transcript but keeps every user and assistant turn
Restarts the session with the same CLAUDE.md loaded and an empty conversation history
Switches to a model with a larger window so the session can continue
questions.explanation: Compaction trades detail for headroom, which is what long sessions need. It summarizes the whole conversation, not just tool results; a clean restart is what /clear does, and it loses the essentials compaction keeps.

questions.question: A developer wants Claude Code to stop before committing so they can review. Best approach?
options: A CLAUDE.md line asking Claude to confirm with the user before running git commit
A PostToolUse hook on git commit that opens the diff for the developer to review
Keep commit outside the allowed actions, or gate it with a hook that requires confirmation
Run the whole session in plan mode so no commands execute until the developer approves the plan
questions.explanation: Review points are enforced through permissions and hooks, not memory. A PostToolUse hook fires after the commit already exists; plan mode blocks all edits, not just the commit.

questions.question: Which of these belongs in CLAUDE.md rather than a subagent or a skill?
options: A 200-page design document describing every subsystem in the product and how they connect
The linter command and a note that the tests need the local database running
A weekly status report template the team fills in every Friday
The API keys for the staging environment so tests can run end to end
questions.explanation: Short, always-relevant operational facts are CLAUDE.md material. Long documents are loaded on demand; a report template is a skill or slash command; keys do not go in a checked-in file.

questions.question: You need Claude Code to review a pull request in CI and post comments, with no ability to push code. Which controls?
options: Print mode with a read-only tool allow list and the git push command denied
Print mode with full permissions, relying on the prompt to say 'do not push code'
Interactive mode on the runner so a reviewer can approve each tool call
Plan mode, since planning cannot push code and can still read the diff
questions.explanation: Least privilege for automation: read-only tools plus explicit denies on writes. Relying on the prompt is advisory; interactive mode has no reviewer present in CI.

questions.question: A Claude Code session is asked to fix a bug and, without being asked, refactors three unrelated files. What reduces this?
options: A larger context window so Claude can see why the other files are unrelated
Running the fix headless so there is no room for exploratory editing
A PostToolUse hook that reverts any edit outside the file named in the prompt
Explicit scope in the prompt, CLAUDE.md conventions about minimal diffs, and plan mode for review
questions.explanation: Scope discipline comes from explicit instructions and a review step before edits. A revert hook is a blunt tool that also blocks legitimate changes in a second file; headless mode removes the review, not the drift.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a PreToolUse hook?
options: Run a command after the model has finished its response
Inspect or block a tool call before it executes
Compact the context when a tool result is too large
Swap the model for a cheaper one on routine tool calls
questions.explanation: Pre hooks gate actions; post hooks react to them. Running after the response is a Stop hook; compaction and model choice are not what hooks control.

questions.question: A system prompt says 'be helpful' and the outputs vary wildly in format. The highest-leverage change is:
options: Adding 'be concise and consistent' to the system prompt
Adding a persona so the model has a stable voice to write in
Stating the exact output format with a short example
Lowering the temperature so the formatting varies less
questions.explanation: Concrete format specification with an example beats abstract adjectives. Lower temperature narrows sampling but cannot supply a format that was never stated; a persona shapes tone, not structure.

questions.question: You need the model to reason through a multi-step pricing rule before answering. Which technique?
options: Ask for the final price only, with a rule that the answer must be a single number
Provide several unrelated worked examples so the model learns to be careful
Split the request across two turns, one for the rule and one for the answer
Ask it to work through the steps before answering, or enable extended thinking for the hard cases
questions.explanation: Letting the model reason before answering improves multi-step accuracy. Asking for the number only removes the working that makes the answer right; unrelated examples teach nothing about this rule.

questions.question: Which is the best use of XML-style tags in a prompt?
options: Separating instructions, reference documents, and examples so the model does not confuse them
Replacing the system prompt with a tagged block at the top of the user turn
Marking the parts of the prompt the model may skip when the context is nearly full
Signalling to the API which sections of the prompt are eligible for prompt caching
questions.explanation: Clear structure prevents content from being read as instructions and makes long prompts unambiguous. Tags are not read by the API for caching; cache_control does that. The model does not skip tagged sections.

questions.question: You want responses to begin with a JSON object and nothing else. Which technique reduces preamble?
options: Setting stop_sequences to a closing brace so the model ends at the object
Prefilling the assistant turn with the opening brace
Adding 'respond with JSON only' as the last line of the system prompt
Setting temperature to zero so the model picks the most likely opening
questions.explanation: Prefilling steers the start of the response and suppresses chatty preambles. A stop sequence controls where the response ends, not where it starts; a 'JSON only' line helps but is still an instruction the model can ignore.

questions.question: The model keeps inventing a citation when a source is missing. Which instruction helps most?
options: 'Cite at least one source for every claim, using the provided material where possible'
'Use your own knowledge to fill gaps when the provided material does not cover a claim'
'Keep answers short so there is less room for unsupported claims to appear'
'If no source in the provided material supports the claim, say so instead of citing'
questions.explanation: Give the model an explicit permitted action for the missing-information case. 'Cite at least one source' is the instruction that produces invented citations; filling gaps from memory replaces one fabrication with another.

questions.question: Which examples make few-shot prompting work best?
options: A few examples that closely match the target task and format, including a tricky edge case
A large set of loosely related examples so the model sees the range of possible inputs
Examples that deliberately contain errors, with corrections, so the model learns what to avoid
Examples drawn from a different but similar domain to avoid overfitting to the test set
questions.explanation: Relevance and quality matter more than quantity; an edge case teaches the boundary. Error-and-correction examples can work for critique tasks, but for a formatting task they put wrong outputs in front of the model.

questions.question: A prompt for summarizing meeting notes should also flag decisions and owners. Where do those requirements go?
options: In a second call after the summary, so each call has one job
Stated explicitly as required output sections, with an example
In the system prompt as a general instruction to 'capture action items'
Implicitly, since a well-written summary includes decisions and owners
questions.explanation: Required elements are stated, structured, and shown, not assumed. A second call is decomposition, which can be fine, but the requirement still has to be stated somewhere; a vague 'action items' line is not a required section.

questions.question: What is the role of the system prompt compared with the user turn?
options: The system prompt is where the model name and version are declared; the user turn holds everything else in the request
The system prompt carries the material to analyze; the user turn carries the standing rules
The system prompt sets standing role, rules, and format; the user turn carries the specific task and material
They are interchangeable; the model concatenates them before reading either
questions.explanation: Separating standing instructions from per-request content keeps prompts stable and cacheable. The reverse split puts volatile material in the cacheable position; the model name is set on the request, not in the prompt.

questions.question: A prompt includes ten rules and the model follows nine. Which change is most effective?
options: Move the missed rule near the task, restate it as a concrete check, and add an example of compliance
Repeat the missed rule in capitals at the top and bottom of the system prompt
Delete the nine rules that already work, so the missed one gets the model's full attention
Move the missed rule into a tool description so the model reads it when it acts
questions.explanation: Position, concreteness, and examples drive rule adherence. Capitals add emphasis without clarity; deleting working rules trades nine known behaviors for one.

questions.question: When should you ask the model to quote the relevant passage before answering a question about a long document?
options: Only for documents short enough that the quotes do not add much to the output
Only when streaming, since the quote arrives first and gives the user something to read while the answer generates
When the answer is a single fact, since longer answers already cite their sources
When accuracy on the document matters, since grounding in quotes reduces invented details
questions.explanation: Quote-then-answer anchors the response in the source, which matters most on long documents. Short documents need it least; streaming is a delivery detail, not a reason.

questions.question: A prompt asks for 'a short answer' and gets three paragraphs. What fixes it reliably?
options: Reduce temperature to zero so the model chooses the most likely, usually shorter, phrasing
Specify the length in sentences or words and show an example of the right length
Set max_tokens to a small value so the response cannot run to three paragraphs
Add 'be brief' to both the system prompt and the user message
questions.explanation: Precise constraints and an example beat vague adjectives. A small max_tokens truncates mid-sentence rather than producing a short answer; temperature does not control length.

questions.question: Which is a sign that a task needs extended thinking rather than a normal response?
options: The prompt is long and contains several reference documents the model has to read through
The user wants the answer quickly and is willing to accept a rough result
The task requires weighing several constraints and checking intermediate steps
The output must follow a strict schema that downstream code will parse
questions.explanation: Extended thinking pays off on multi-constraint reasoning, not on lookups. A long prompt is a context question, not a reasoning one; a strict schema is solved by structured output.

questions.question: What is a good way to make a prompt testable?
options: Keep the prompt general so it holds up on inputs you did not anticipate
Freeze the prompt once it works and route changes through a new prompt
Test it against live traffic and roll back when the error rate rises
Define expected outputs for a set of inputs and check the prompt against them after every change
questions.explanation: A prompt with a test set can be improved safely; one without cannot. Live traffic tests find problems after users see them; freezing the prompt avoids regressions by refusing improvements.

questions.question: Which change most often improves a prompt that is 'almost right'?
options: Replacing an ambiguous instruction with a specific, checkable one
Adding a persona that matches the domain the prompt operates in
Adding a line asking the model to double-check its answer before responding
Moving the instructions from the system prompt into the user turn
questions.explanation: Ambiguity is the usual culprit; specificity is the usual fix. A double-check line can help on reasoning tasks but does not tell the model what it misunderstood; a persona shapes voice, not correctness.

questions.question: Two tools, search_customers and find_customers, do nearly the same thing and the model picks inconsistently. What should you do?
options: Add a routing instruction to the system prompt that says which tool to prefer
Merge them into one well-described tool, or make their purposes clearly distinct in name and description
Set tool_choice to the preferred tool so the model no longer has to choose
Keep both and add a third tool that wraps them and picks the right one internally
questions.explanation: Overlapping tools confuse selection; fewer, clearly scoped tools work better. Forcing tool_choice removes the model's choice on every turn, including turns where no tool is needed; a wrapper tool adds a third overlapping name.

questions.question: A tool returns a 4 MB JSON dump on every call and the agent's context fills quickly. Best fix?
options: Compress the JSON before returning it so it occupies fewer tokens in context
Call the tool less often by caching its output in the system prompt for the session
Ask the model to summarize each result before continuing so the raw dump is dropped
Return only the fields the task needs, paginate, and let the model request more
questions.explanation: Tools should return concise, meaningful context, not raw dumps. Compressing JSON does not reduce tokens meaningfully; having the model summarize still costs the full dump in context first.

questions.question: Which naming convention helps a model with many tools?
options: Consistent namespacing by system, such as crm_search and crm_update
Short names of one or two characters so the tool list stays compact
Names that describe the return type, such as list_result and single_result
Names that include the version, such as search_v2, so the model picks the latest
questions.explanation: Predictable, namespaced names make the tool surface legible to the model. Return-type names say nothing about purpose; version suffixes ask the model to guess which one is current.

questions.question: An MCP server exposes a 'prompts' primitive. What is it for?
options: Instructions the server injects into the client's system prompt on connect
The templates a tool uses to format its own results before returning them
Reusable prompt templates the client can discover and invoke
The configuration block that tells the client how to authenticate and transport
questions.explanation: MCP has tools, resources, and prompts; prompts are reusable templates the client exposes to the user. Servers do not inject text into the client's system prompt; authentication and transport are handled outside the primitives.

questions.question: A remote MCP server holds customer data. Which is required?
options: Running the server over stdio through an SSH tunnel so that no HTTP endpoint is ever exposed to the network
Storing an API key in the tool description so the model can present it on each call
Restricting the server to read-only tools so a compromised client cannot change data
Authentication and authorization on the server, with the client presenting credentials
questions.explanation: Remote servers with sensitive data need auth like any other service. Read-only tools still leak customer data to anyone who connects; a key in the tool description is visible to every client and the model.

questions.question: What should a tool's description include beyond what it does?
options: The server it lives on and the endpoint it calls, so the model can troubleshoot failures
When to use it and when not to, parameter meanings, and edge cases
The expected latency and rate limits so the model can plan parallel calls
The list of other tools that must be called before it, so ordering is explicit
questions.explanation: The description is the model's decision guide for the tool. Endpoint details and latency are operational data the model cannot act on; a required call order is better expressed by returning what the next call needs than by a list the model has to track.

questions.question: A tool has a 'delete' action and a 'read' action behind one parameter. Why is that a design problem?
options: Read-only and destructive actions need different gating; split them so the destructive one can be permissioned separately
Enum parameters are poorly supported in JSON Schema, so the model will often pass an invalid value
One parameter cannot carry two verbs, so the schema will fail validation on the API
The model will default to the first enum value, so reads will be attempted as deletes
questions.explanation: Separating safe and dangerous operations lets you gate the dangerous one. Enums are well supported and the schema is valid; the problem is not the schema but the fact that a permission rule cannot tell a read from a delete.

questions.question: The model calls a tool with a date in the wrong format, repeatedly. Best fix?
options: Accept any format the model sends and normalize it inside the tool, so the loop never stalls
Remove the date parameter and have the tool default to today, asking the user for other dates
Add a schema format hint and an example value in the description, and return a clear error on bad input
Add a system prompt rule stating the date format, since the model reads the tool description less carefully
questions.explanation: Schema hints, examples, and actionable errors fix malformed calls. Silent normalization hides a defect that will bite when a date is ambiguous; the tool description is exactly where the model looks when it builds the call.

questions.question: When is parallel tool use appropriate?
options: When the tools belong to the same MCP server, so one connection can batch them
When the calls are independent and the results do not depend on one another
When latency matters, regardless of whether one call's input comes from another
When the model is confident about all the arguments before the first result returns
questions.explanation: Independent calls can run concurrently; dependent ones cannot. Latency is the motivation, not the condition; if one call needs another's output, it has to wait. The server they belong to is irrelevant.

questions.question: Which is a resource in MCP terms?
options: A function the model can call to change state on the server
A reusable template the user selects to start a conversation
The transport the client uses to reach the server, such as stdio or streamable HTTP
Data the client can read, like a file or a record, addressed by URI
questions.explanation: Resources are readable data; tools are callable actions; prompts are templates. Transport is how the client connects, not one of the three primitives.

questions.question: A tool should be idempotent when:
options: Its effects must be safe to repeat, because agent loops retry
It only reads data, since reads are the calls the loop repeats most
It runs over stdio, where a dropped connection replays the call
It has no parameters, so every call is identical by construction
questions.explanation: Retries are normal; idempotency makes them harmless. Read-only tools are already idempotent by nature; the property matters for tools with side effects. Transport does not replay calls.

questions.question: What is the safest default for a new tool that writes to an external system?
options: Autonomous use with a nightly report of what it wrote, so problems surface within a day
Disabled in production and enabled only in a staging environment until accuracy is measured
Requires confirmation until its accuracy is measured
Autonomous use for small writes and confirmation for large ones, with the threshold set by the model
questions.explanation: Start gated; expand autonomy on evidence. Staging-only means no real accuracy data; letting the model set its own threshold makes the model the gate again.

questions.question: What is 'context rot'?
options: A caching bug in which a stale cached prefix is served after the system prompt has changed
The decline in response quality as the window fills with stale or irrelevant content
The gradual loss of tool results when compaction summarizes older turns
The drift in a model's behavior over weeks as the provider updates it
questions.explanation: Recognizing context rot is why compaction and clearing exist. It is about what is in the window now, not a caching fault or model updates; compaction is the cure, not the cause.

questions.question: An agent needs occasional access to a 500-page manual. Best approach?
options: Load the whole manual into every prompt and rely on prompt caching to keep it cheap
Summarize it once into a few pages and give the agent only the summary
Index it and retrieve relevant sections on demand, giving the model identifiers it can fetch
Split it into ten chunks and run a subagent per chunk on every question
questions.explanation: Just-in-time retrieval keeps the window lean and accurate. Caching makes the full manual cheaper but not free, and 500 pages of mostly irrelevant text still degrades attention; a one-time summary loses the details the occasional question needs.

questions.question: Which content should sit at the start of the prompt for prompt caching to help?
options: The user's latest question, so the model reads it before the long material
The stable system prompt and tool definitions
The most recent tool results, since those are reused across turns
The conversation history, since it is the largest part of the request
questions.explanation: Cache hits depend on a stable prefix. Tool results and the latest question change every turn, so placing them first breaks the prefix for every request.

questions.question: A long-running agent needs to remember decisions across sessions. Which mechanism fits?
options: A longer system prompt that lists the decisions made so far
A larger max_tokens value so the agent can restate all of its decisions in each response
Prompt caching on the previous session's transcript so it is cheap to include
A memory file or structured notes the agent reads at start and updates as it works
questions.explanation: Persistence across sessions needs an explicit store the agent maintains. Caching a transcript keeps it cheap to send but does not curate it, and the cache expires; a system prompt edited by hand is memory the agent cannot update.

questions.question: Why hand a subagent a task instead of doing everything in one context?
options: Subagents run on a different model, so the main session's model stays available
Subagents can call tools the main session is not allowed to use
The subagent's working context stays separate and only its conclusion returns, preserving the main window
Subagents share the main session's context, so they start with full knowledge of the task
questions.explanation: Context isolation is the main benefit of delegation. Subagents do not share the main context, which is the point; the model and tool set can be configured but are not why you delegate.

questions.question: A prompt includes the full history of a two-hour support chat. Most of it is resolved. What should you do?
options: Summarize the resolved parts and keep the open issue verbatim
Keep the full history, since the model may need context from resolved issues
Drop the history and restate the open issue in a fresh prompt
Keep the last twenty messages and drop everything before them
questions.explanation: Summarize the settled, keep the live. Keeping everything wastes the window on closed threads; a fixed tail of twenty messages may cut through the middle of the open issue.

questions.question: Which is a symptom that a context window is being wasted?
options: Frequent cache hits on the system prompt across many consecutive requests from the same client
Large tool results the model never uses and repeated boilerplate in every turn
Short prompts that leave most of the window empty
Responses that arrive faster than the previous session's
questions.explanation: Unused bulk and repetition are the usual waste. Cache hits and fast responses are signs of a healthy prompt; empty headroom is not waste.

questions.question: What is the trade-off of aggressive summarization in an agent loop?
options: Summaries make later turns slower because the model must reconstruct the details
Summaries break tool use because tool_result blocks cannot be summarized
Headroom and speed at the cost of detail, so keep exact values and identifiers later steps need
Summaries are safe as long as the summary is written by a larger model
questions.explanation: Summaries lose detail; preserve what downstream steps depend on. Later turns are usually faster with a shorter context, not slower, and tool results can be summarized like anything else.

questions.question: Which information should be kept verbatim through compaction?
options: The greetings and pleasantries, since tone carries across turns
The earliest turns, since they set up the task
Resolved errors and their stack traces, in case they recur
Identifiers, exact values, and the current task definition
questions.explanation: Precision-critical items survive; chatter does not. The earliest turns matter only for the task definition, which is what is kept; resolved errors are exactly what a summary can compress.

questions.question: A team wants to cut cost on a chat product with a long, stable system prompt and many short user turns. First lever?
options: Prompt caching on the system prompt and tool definitions
Trimming the system prompt to a few lines so every request is smaller
Batching user turns so several are answered in one request
Switching to a smaller model for every turn after the first
questions.explanation: Caching the stable prefix is the cheapest win for that shape. Trimming the system prompt may cost quality; batching turns breaks the chat experience; a smaller model changes the product.

questions.question: What does 'give the agent lightweight identifiers' mean in context engineering?
options: Use short variable and file names in the code the agent works on so tokens are saved
Replace user names with anonymous ids before content reaches the model
Pass file paths, record ids, and URLs so the agent can fetch details when needed instead of front-loading everything
Give each tool a short alias so the tool list occupies fewer tokens
questions.explanation: Identifiers enable on-demand retrieval. Short names and tool aliases save a handful of tokens; anonymization is a privacy measure, not a context strategy.

questions.question: How should an architect decide the context budget for a step in a workflow?
options: Use the model's maximum on every step so no step runs out of room
From what the step must read and produce, leaving headroom for tool results and reasoning
Split the total window evenly across the steps in the workflow
Reuse the budget from the last project that used the same model
questions.explanation: Budget from the step's real needs, with headroom. An even split starves the heavy steps and pads the light ones; the maximum on every step invites bloat and cost.

questions.question: A due-diligence agent must read 300 contracts and produce one risk table. Which structure keeps quality consistent?
options: Chain the contracts sequentially so each worker sees the previous worker's risk rows before extracting its own
Load all 300 contracts into one long context and ask for a single risk table in one pass
Fan out one worker per contract with the same extraction brief and schema, then merge the structured results
Route each contract by type to a specialist prompt and let each specialist write its own section of the table
questions.explanation: Uniform per-item briefs and structured returns make fan-out work reproducible and mergeable. Chaining contracts sequentially lets early errors contaminate later extractions and adds no consistency; routing by type produces sections written to different standards.

questions.question: What is the main cost of adding a 'reflection' step where the agent critiques its own output before returning it?
options: Added tokens and latency, so it pays off where errors are expensive and the criteria are checkable
The critique tends to anchor on the draft, so it should replace the generator rather than follow it
It blocks tool use during the critique turn, so agents that rely on tools cannot use reflection safely
It only works with a larger model as the critic, which doubles the cost of every task in the pipeline
questions.explanation: Self-critique costs tokens and time, so it belongs on high-stakes, checkable work and wastes budget elsewhere. A critic does not need a larger model, does not block tools, and is meant to follow the generator, not replace it.

questions.question: An agent is allowed to call a payments API. Which control is non-negotiable?
options: A detailed tool description that lists the payment limits so the model knows when to refuse a transfer
A system prompt instruction to confirm the amount with the user before every payment call
An evaluator model that reviews each proposed payment call and rejects any that look unusual
An enforced gate outside the model that requires approval or applies limits before the call executes
questions.explanation: Money moves only through gates enforced in code, not on the model's judgment. Descriptions, prompt instructions, and an evaluator model all rely on a model following guidance, which is not a hard control.

questions.question: Which sign suggests a workflow should be split into two chained model calls?
options: The prompt calls a single tool several times per run, and each call returns a large result
One prompt both extracts facts and writes persuasive prose, and one of those two keeps degrading
Outputs are short and consistent, but the prompt is longer than the team would like to maintain
The task takes several seconds per run, and latency matters more than accuracy for this use case
questions.explanation: Competing objectives in one call degrade both; chaining separates extraction from writing. Large tool results are a context problem, not a chaining signal, and chaining adds latency rather than removing it.

questions.question: A team runs an agent that reads email and drafts replies. A client asks why it never sends automatically. Best answer?
options: Sending is irreversible and public, so it stays gated by a person until measured accuracy earns more autonomy
The Messages API has no outbound email capability of its own, so a person has to press send in the mail client each time
Autonomous sending would break prompt caching because each sent message changes the conversation prefix
The agent runs in a workflow rather than an agent loop, and workflows cannot trigger external actions
questions.explanation: Autonomy follows evidence; irreversible actions start gated. Sending is a tool the team could add at any time, so the limit is a design choice, not an API or caching constraint.

questions.question: What distinguishes routing from an orchestrator in the workflow patterns?
options: Routing requires a separate model per path, while an orchestrator uses one model for every subtask
Routing runs several fixed paths in parallel and merges their outputs; an orchestrator runs the same paths one after another and keeps the best
Routing sends an input down one of several fixed paths; an orchestrator plans dynamic subtasks and synthesizes results
Routing is a form of parallelization; an orchestrator is a form of evaluator-optimizer loop
questions.explanation: Routing classifies an input and picks a fixed path; orchestration plans subtasks that were not known in advance and merges the results. Running paths in parallel and merging describes parallelization, not routing.

questions.question: An agent produced a correct answer but took 40 tool calls where 5 would do. Which lever addresses this?
options: Cut the tool list down to the two or three tools the task used most, so there is less to choose from and fewer wrong turns
Sharper tool descriptions, an explicit plan step, and a per-task call budget with feedback as it nears the limit
Lower the context window by trimming the system prompt so the model has less to reason over each turn
Switch to parallel tool calls so the 40 calls complete in the time five sequential ones would take
questions.explanation: Tool clarity, planning, and budgets reduce thrashing. Removing tools may break other tasks, and parallel calls hide the waste instead of removing it.

questions.question: Why should a subagent's brief include the success criteria and the expected return format?
options: Because the Agent SDK rejects a subagent definition that has no output schema attached
So the subagent can skip tool calls and answer from the brief alone, saving tokens
So the coordinator can reuse the subagent's full transcript as context for later steps instead of a lossy summary
So the subagent knows when to stop and the coordinator can merge results without re-reading transcripts
questions.explanation: Clear criteria and formats make delegation composable: the worker stops at the right point and the coordinator merges structured returns. Reusing full transcripts is the thing a good brief avoids.

questions.question: A stakeholder asks for 'an AI that runs the whole department'. As the architect, the first design move is:
options: Pick the most capable model available so the agent can handle whatever the department throws at it
Build one general agent with every department tool attached and let it learn the workflows from use
Start with an orchestrator-workers system so each function of the department gets its own dedicated worker agent
Map the workflows, classify steps by predictability and blast radius, and start with the predictable ones
questions.explanation: Decompose, classify, and start where reliability is easy to prove. Jumping to an orchestrator or a single general agent commits to an architecture before the work has been understood.

questions.question: Which is the correct role of an evaluator in an evaluator-optimizer loop?
options: Produce the first draft, then revise it against the same criteria in a single turn
Judge the draft against explicit criteria and return specific, actionable feedback
Decide which tools the generator may call on its next attempt at the task
Summarize the generator's transcript so the loop fits in the context window
questions.explanation: Evaluators judge against criteria and feed back; generators produce. Drafting and revising in one turn is self-critique, not the two-role loop.

questions.question: An agent needs to process items that arrive continuously over a day. What design fits?
options: A queue-driven loop that handles each item in a fresh bounded context and persists state between items
One long-running session that keeps every item in context so it can spot patterns across the day
A single batch prompt at the end of the day that processes all items together in one call
An orchestrator that spawns a subagent per item and keeps every subagent transcript for the coordinator
questions.explanation: Per-item bounded contexts with persisted state scale and stay reliable. A day-long session overflows, an end-of-day batch loses timeliness, and keeping every transcript in the coordinator recreates the overflow.

questions.question: What is the practical reason to make agent steps observable with structured logs rather than free-text notes?
options: Free-text notes consume more tokens per step, so structured logs keep the run inside the context budget
The model produces more consistent reasoning when it is asked to log in a structured format
Structured logs can be queried, rolled into metrics, and replayed for evaluation
Structured logs are required for prompt caching to work across steps of the run
questions.explanation: Structure makes behavior measurable and replayable. Logs live outside the context window, so token savings and caching are not the reason.

questions.question: A coordinator receives conflicting answers from two subagents. Sound handling?
options: Take the answer from whichever subagent used more tool calls, since it did more research
Detect the conflict, resolve it with a defined rule or a verification step, and record the decision
Merge both answers into one combined response and let the downstream consumer decide which parts to trust
Rerun both subagents with the same brief and accept the answer that appears more often
questions.explanation: Conflicts need explicit resolution and a record, not a silent choice. Tool-call count is not evidence of correctness, and majority reruns can repeat the same error.

questions.question: Which situation calls for human-in-the-loop by design rather than by exception?
options: Approving legal commitments, spending above a threshold, or changes to people's records
Any step where the model reports low confidence in its own answer partway through the run
Every tool call that reads from a production database rather than a staging copy
Steps where two workers in a parallel fan-out return different formatting
questions.explanation: High-consequence categories get a standing human step. Low model confidence triggers a review by exception, and reads or formatting mismatches are handled in code.

questions.question: What is the risk of letting an agent modify its own instructions during a run?
options: The run costs more because each instruction rewrite invalidates the cached prompt prefix
The agent becomes slower to complete tasks because it spends turns editing its own prompt
Drift and loss of control; standing instructions should be fixed, versioned, and changed by people
There is little risk if every instruction change is logged, since the log lets you replay the run afterward
questions.explanation: Self-modifying instructions undermine predictability and audit. Cache and speed costs are minor by comparison, and logging a drift does not prevent it.

questions.question: A workflow's third step frequently fails on malformed input from step two. Best fix?
options: Validate step two's output against a schema before step three runs, with a repair path on failure
Wrap step three in a retry loop with backoff so transient formatting problems resolve themselves
Merge steps two and three into one prompt so there is no boundary for malformed data to cross
Ask step three to tolerate malformed input by instructing it to do its best with whatever arrives
questions.explanation: Validate at boundaries; repair or route on failure. Retries do not fix deterministic malformation, and merging steps hides the fault instead of catching it.

questions.question: A monorepo has several services with different test commands. Where should that live for Claude Code?
options: A subagent per service that carries that service's commands in its own prompt
The repository README, which Claude Code reads automatically at session start
The first message of each session, restated whenever the service changes
CLAUDE.md, with a short per-service map of test commands and conventions
questions.explanation: Project memory holds per-area commands and loads on every session. The README is not loaded automatically, and restating commands in chat is manual and easy to forget.

questions.question: Which hook event would you use to run a security scan on every file Claude writes?
options: A PreToolUse hook on the Read tool, so files are scanned before Claude opens them
A PostToolUse hook matched to the Write and Edit tools, run after each change lands
A Stop hook that scans the whole working tree once when Claude finishes its turn and reports findings
A slash command the developer runs after each session to scan changed files
questions.explanation: Post hooks react to completed writes, so the scan sees the file as written. A Stop hook runs once per turn and misses intermediate writes; a PreToolUse hook on Read never sees writes at all.

questions.question: A developer wants Claude Code to ask before running any command that touches the network. Which setting?
options: Permission rules that allow safe commands and require confirmation for matching network commands
A PostToolUse hook on Bash that inspects the command for network calls and logs a warning
A CLAUDE.md instruction telling Claude to ask for confirmation before any command that reaches the network
Plan mode for the whole session, so every command is proposed before it is executed
questions.explanation: Granular permission rules gate specific commands. A PostToolUse hook runs after the command has already executed, and a CLAUDE.md line is guidance rather than enforcement.

questions.question: What is the benefit of committing project-scoped MCP configuration to the repo?
options: It lets the repo's MCP servers override the user's own server settings for the project
Server credentials travel with the code, so contributors do not need their own tokens
Every contributor gets the same integrations without manual setup on each machine
Claude Code caches the server tool lists in git, which speeds up session start
questions.explanation: Shared config travels with the code, so integrations are consistent across the team. Credentials should stay out of the repo, in environment variables or user-level config.

questions.question: Claude Code proposes a plan that touches an unrelated module. What is the right response in plan mode?
options: Accept the plan, then revert the unrelated edits during code review
Exit plan mode and let Claude discover the right scope as it edits
Revise the plan's scope before any edits are made to the tree
Run the test suite first to see whether the extra module is affected
questions.explanation: Plan mode exists to correct scope before edits happen. Accepting and reverting later wastes work and risks missing an edit.

questions.question: Which is a sensible use of a Claude Code skill?
options: A packaged procedure like 'write a release note from merged PRs' with its own instructions and helper files
A replacement for CLAUDE.md that holds all project conventions and commands in a single file loaded on demand
A place to store the API keys and tokens the procedure needs, loaded only when invoked
A per-task override that switches the session to a different model for that procedure
questions.explanation: Skills package reusable procedures with their supporting files. Project conventions belong in CLAUDE.md, and secrets belong in environment configuration, not in a skill.

questions.question: You want a nightly job where Claude Code triages new issues and labels them. Which pieces?
options: An interactive session left open overnight with auto-accept enabled for all tool calls
Print mode in a scheduled job with a read-only tool set plus one allowed labeling action
A PostToolUse hook that fires whenever a new issue is created and labels it in place
A subagent with full permissions, invoked from a cron entry with the issue list as input
questions.explanation: Headless, scheduled, and least-privilege. Hooks respond to Claude's own tool calls, not to external events, and full permissions are more than a labeling job needs.

questions.question: A PreToolUse hook exits with code 2 on a tool call. What should happen?
options: The call proceeds and the hook's stderr is shown to the user, as with other non-zero exits
Claude Code ends the session so the developer can inspect the hook's output manually
The hook is disabled for the rest of the session and the call is retried once
The call is blocked and the hook's message is surfaced so the model can adjust
questions.explanation: Exit code 2 is the blocking exit: the action stops and the hook's stderr is fed back to the model. Other non-zero codes surface the message to the user and let the call continue.

questions.question: Which practice keeps a long Claude Code session productive?
options: Clearing or compacting between unrelated tasks and re-briefing the next task
Pasting the previous session's transcript at the start so no earlier decision is lost
Disabling hooks mid-session so tool calls complete with less overhead
Keeping one session open so the model keeps every file it has read
questions.explanation: Fresh context per task keeps attention on what matters. Pasting transcripts or holding every file read fills the window with material the next task does not need.

questions.question: What should a team review when a Claude Code change is opened as a pull request?
options: The commit message and the model version, since the diff itself was generated
The test output only, because a green suite proves the change is correct
Whether the CLAUDE.md conventions were followed, with the diff left to CI
The diff, the tests it ran, and whether the scope matched the request
questions.explanation: Review automated changes like any other: the diff, the evidence, and the scope. A green suite does not prove the change did what was asked.

questions.question: Which is the right place for a rule like 'never edit files under vendor/'?
options: A README section, since Claude Code reads project documentation before it edits
A dedicated subagent that owns vendor/ and rejects edit requests from the main session
CLAUDE.md for guidance plus a hook or permission deny rule for enforcement
A comment at the top of each vendored file saying the file is not to be edited
questions.explanation: Guidance plus enforcement: CLAUDE.md explains the rule and a deny rule or hook makes it hold. File comments and READMEs are only read if Claude happens to open them.

questions.question: How do subagents help with a large migration in Claude Code?
options: They share the main session's context, so every slice sees the same file history and the same earlier decisions
Each handles a bounded slice in its own context and returns a summary, keeping the main session coherent
They run without tools, so they can plan slices while the main session performs the edits
They bypass the test suite for each slice so the migration completes faster
questions.explanation: Bounded slices with summaries back keep the coordinator's window clean. Subagents have separate contexts and can use tools; sharing context is the problem they solve.

questions.question: Which instruction most improves factual grounding when documents are provided?
options: 'Answer only from the provided documents and cite the passage; if it is not there, say so'
'You are a careful analyst who values accuracy above all else in every answer you give'
'Combine the documents with your own knowledge and give the most complete answer'
'Be concise and accurate, and avoid speculation unless the user asks for it'
questions.explanation: Explicit grounding plus a permitted 'not found' path is what stops the model filling gaps. A persona of an accurate analyst sets tone but gives the model no rule for missing facts.

questions.question: A prompt must produce output in a strict template across thousands of runs. Which combination is strongest?
options: A detailed persona plus a high temperature so the model stays engaged across runs
A long narrative description of the task that explains why the template matters
A precise template, one or two examples, and schema enforcement where possible
Ten varied examples with no explicit template, so the model infers the pattern
questions.explanation: Specification, examples, and enforcement. Examples alone leave the model to infer the template, and varied examples pull output in different directions.

questions.question: What is the drawback of stuffing every possible rule into one system prompt?
options: Longer system prompts break prompt caching, so each run pays full price for the rules
There is no real drawback as long as the rules are numbered and grouped by topic
The model treats later rules as higher priority, so the early rules get ignored
Rules compete and get missed; prioritize, structure, and test which ones matter
questions.explanation: More rules is not more adherence; rules compete for attention. A long stable system prompt caches well, so caching is not the drawback.

questions.question: When should you show the model a negative example (what not to do)?
options: In every prompt, paired with each positive example so the contrast is explicit
When a specific failure keeps recurring and a positive example alone has not fixed it
Only in the system prompt, since negatives in the user turn are treated as content
Only as a last resort after temperature and max_tokens adjustments have both failed to help
questions.explanation: Targeted negatives address stubborn failure modes. Pairing a negative with every positive adds noise and can draw attention to the wrong behavior.

questions.question: Which is the best way to get the model to ask a clarifying question instead of guessing?
options: Lower the temperature so the model is less willing to commit to an uncertain answer
Instruct it to ask when a required detail is missing, and define what counts as required
Include examples of confident guesses marked as wrong so the model learns to avoid them in similar cases
Add a persona of a cautious consultant who checks with the client before acting
questions.explanation: Define the condition for asking. A cautious persona shifts tone but does not tell the model which details are required.

questions.question: A summarization prompt is losing important numbers. What helps?
options: Ask for a shorter summary so the model focuses on only the most important facts
Switch to bullet points, since lists make omitted figures easier for a reader to spot
Increase max_tokens so the summary has room for every number in the source
Instruct it to preserve all figures, dates, and names verbatim, with an example
questions.explanation: Name what must survive and show it. Extra output room does not tell the model that figures matter, and a shorter summary drops more of them.

questions.question: What does 'role prompting' do well and what does it not fix?
options: It improves factual accuracy by activating domain expertise the model would not otherwise use
It replaces the need for examples, since a strong persona implies the expected output
It sets tone and perspective; it does not fix missing instructions, data, or ambiguous tasks
It fixes ambiguous tasks by giving the model a viewpoint from which to resolve them
questions.explanation: Personas shape voice, not correctness. A role does not supply missing data or resolve an ambiguous task definition.

questions.question: Which prompt is more testable?
options: 'Write a summary of at most 120 words with one sentence per section, listing every decision and owner'
'Write a thorough, well-organized summary that a busy executive would find genuinely useful and complete'
'Summarize this document in the style of our best analyst, keeping the reader's needs in mind'
