'Produce a high-quality summary and double-check it for completeness before you answer'
questions.explanation: Concrete constraints can be checked: word count, sentence count, decisions and owners. 'Useful' and 'high-quality' cannot be scored without a rubric.

questions.question: You want the model to output only 'APPROVE' or 'REJECT'. What is the most reliable approach?
options: Raise max_tokens and instruct the model to end its response with the final label on its own line
Add a strict reviewer persona and ask the model to be decisive in every answer it gives
Constrain the output through an enum in a tool schema, or prefill and instruct with examples
Ask the question twice and accept the label only when both responses agree with each other
questions.explanation: Enforce the label set with a schema or prefill. A label on the last line still needs parsing and can be preceded by unwanted text.

questions.question: How should a prompt handle ambiguous user requests in a customer-facing product?
options: Instruct the model to state its interpretation or ask one clarifying question, per product policy
Instruct the model to answer every plausible interpretation in turn so the user can pick the right one
Instruct the model to decline ambiguous requests and direct the user to a support form
Instruct the model to choose the most common interpretation and answer with confidence
questions.explanation: Explicit ambiguity handling, matched to product policy. Answering every interpretation is long and confusing, and confident guesses hide the ambiguity from the user.

questions.question: Which change is likely to reduce hallucinated tool parameters?
options: Fewer examples in the tool description, so the model relies on the schema alone
Examples of correct calls in the tool description and a schema with enums and required fields
A system prompt persona of a careful engineer who double-checks every parameter before calling a tool
Longer output budgets so the model has room to reason before it commits to a call
questions.explanation: Show correct calls and constrain the schema. A careful persona does not tell the model which values are valid.

questions.question: What is a reasonable way to iterate on a prompt with a team?
options: One owner edits the production prompt by feel and watches user feedback for regressions
Freeze the prompt after launch and route new requirements to a separate prompt
Each teammate tests edits in their own environment and merges whichever version feels best
Versioned prompts, a shared eval set, and review of score changes before deploy
questions.explanation: Treat prompts like code: versioned, evaluated on a shared set, and reviewed. Merging by feel has no shared measure of better.

questions.question: A tool takes 20 optional parameters and the model rarely sets them correctly. Best redesign?
options: Make every parameter required so the model has to think about each one explicitly
Split into focused tools with few required parameters and sensible defaults
Move the parameter guidance into the system prompt so it is not lost in the schema
Keep the tool but add a validation step that rejects calls with unset parameters
questions.explanation: Narrow tools with few parameters are easier to call correctly. Making all 20 required makes every call harder, and validation catches errors without reducing them.

questions.question: What should a search tool return to be most useful to an agent?
options: Every matching record in full, so the agent never needs a second call
A count of matches with a suggestion to narrow the query whenever the count is above a threshold
The raw response from the underlying search service, unmodified
A compact ranked list with identifiers and snippets, plus a way to fetch details
questions.explanation: Compact, actionable, and fetchable. Full records flood the context, and a count alone gives the agent nothing to act on.

questions.question: Which MCP capability lets a server suggest a full workflow prompt to the client?
options: Prompts, which are reusable templates the client can present for the user to invoke
Resources, which expose text or data the client can load into context by URI when it needs it
Tools, which return a suggested plan the client then executes step by step
Sampling, which lets the server request a completion from the client's model
questions.explanation: Prompts are reusable templates exposed by servers. Resources expose data, tools perform actions, and sampling runs in the other direction.

questions.question: A tool's description says 'Use this for anything related to customers'. Why is that weak?
options: It is too short; a description should run to several paragraphs to cover every case
It fails to list the parameter types, so the model cannot construct a valid call
It is too broad: it invites misuse and overlaps with other tools; describe the job and when not to use it
It is phrased as an instruction to the model, when descriptions should be neutral statements of what the tool does and returns
questions.explanation: Specificity guides selection. Parameter types belong in the schema, and length alone does not make a description useful.

questions.question: When should a tool return an error rather than a best-effort result?
options: When the input is invalid or the operation cannot complete correctly, with a message saying what would fix it
Only on timeouts and network failures; for bad input, return the closest valid result with a note explaining the substitution
Whenever the operation partially succeeds, so the model retries the whole call from scratch
Only when the model has asked for strict mode; otherwise return a best-effort result silently
questions.explanation: Honest errors beat silent partials, and an actionable message lets the model correct the call. Returning the closest valid result for bad input hides the problem from the model.

questions.question: Which is true of tool_result blocks?
options: They are placed in the system prompt so the model sees them on every later turn
They must contain valid JSON so the model can parse them reliably
They replace the assistant's tool_use block in the conversation history
They are returned in a user turn, matched to the tool_use block's id
questions.explanation: Results come back in the next user turn, matched by id to the tool_use block, which stays in the history. Content can be text, JSON, or images; JSON is not required.

questions.question: How do you keep an MCP server safe when it exposes both read and write operations?
options: Expose write operations only over stdio, since local transport limits who can call them
Trust the model's judgment on each call but log every write so problems can be traced and reversed afterward
Separate read and write tools, require authentication, and gate writes with confirmation or scopes
Combine reads and writes in one tool with a mode flag so the model sees fewer tools
questions.explanation: Separate the tools, authenticate callers, and gate writes. A mode flag makes it easier to write by accident, and logging after the fact does not prevent damage.

questions.question: A model keeps calling a tool that is not relevant to the task. Which fix comes first?
options: Delete the tool from the set, since a tool that gets misused is a net cost
Tighten its description with 'when not to use' guidance and check for overlap with other tools
Lower the temperature so the model becomes more conservative about tool selection
Add a system prompt rule that lists the exact tasks the tool may be used for and the tasks it may not
questions.explanation: Descriptions drive selection, so fix the description and any overlap first. A system prompt rule can help but is further from the point of choice than the tool's own description.

questions.question: Why include units and formats in parameter descriptions?
options: The MCP specification requires units in every numeric parameter description
They are mainly for the humans who review tool calls in the logs
They let the model skip the schema and construct calls from the description alone
So the model supplies values the tool can parse, avoiding silent errors
questions.explanation: Precision prevents malformed calls, such as seconds passed where milliseconds were expected. Descriptions are model-facing, and the schema still applies.

questions.question: What is a good reason to expose a resource instead of a tool?
options: The data is read-only reference material the client can load on demand by URI
The data changes every second and the client needs the freshest possible copy
Loading the data has side effects that should be visible in the audit log
Access to the data requires a human approval step before it is released
questions.explanation: Read-only reference data suits resources. Side effects and approval gates are tool concerns.

questions.question: A prompt is 150k tokens and quality is uneven. What is the first question to ask?
options: Whether a newer model with a larger context window would handle the same 150k tokens more evenly
Whether raising max_tokens would give the model more room to work through the material
How much of that context the task needs, and whether retrieval or summarization could replace the bulk
Whether the prompt has a clear persona so the model knows how to weigh the material
questions.explanation: Budget the context from what the task needs; retrieval or summarization usually replaces the bulk. A larger window carries the same irrelevant material, and max_tokens affects output, not input.

questions.question: What goes in a memory file that an agent maintains across sessions?
options: Full transcripts of each session so nothing is lost between runs
Decisions, open items, and pointers to sources, kept short and current
Every tool result, so the agent can avoid repeating calls it already made
Credentials and endpoints the agent needs, so it can start without setup
questions.explanation: Durable, compact state. Transcripts and tool results bloat the file, and credentials belong in secure configuration.

questions.question: Which practice supports prompt caching across many users of the same app?
options: Put each user's profile at the start of the system prompt so it is cached per user
Disable the system prompt and pass all instructions in the first user message
Randomize the order of instructions so no single prefix dominates the cache
A shared stable prefix, with user-specific content after the cache breakpoint
questions.explanation: Shared prefix first, user content after. Putting the profile first makes every user's prefix different, so nothing is shared.

questions.question: How should long tool outputs be handled in an agent loop?
options: Truncated or summarized to the essentials, keeping identifiers so details can be re-fetched
Kept in full, since dropping any part of a tool result risks losing something the task needs
Moved into the system prompt so they are cached and do not consume the conversation budget
Deleted after the turn that used them, since the model has already acted on them
questions.explanation: Keep the essentials and the pointers. Full outputs crowd out later reasoning, and deleting them outright loses details a later step may need.

questions.question: What is a reasonable trigger for compaction in a long session?
options: After every message, so the window stays as small as possible
Approaching the context budget or finishing a subtask
Only when a tool call fails, since errors usually mean the context is polluted
Only when the user asks, since the model cannot judge when to compact
questions.explanation: Compact at natural boundaries or near limits. Compacting every message loses detail constantly for no benefit.

questions.question: Why can a smaller, curated context beat a larger one?
options: Models are trained on short prompts, so long prompts fall outside the distribution
The claim does not hold; more context is better as long as it fits inside the model's window
Less irrelevant material means better attention to what matters, alongside lower cost
Smaller contexts are cheaper, and the cost saving is the only real difference
questions.explanation: Relevance beats volume: irrelevant material competes for attention. Cost is a bonus, not the only difference.

questions.question: An agent must reference a style guide on every task. Where does it belong?
options: In the stable prefix so it caches, or loaded once per session
Pasted into each user message so it is always the most recent input
Returned through a tool result on the first turn of each task
Summarized to one line in the system prompt to save tokens
questions.explanation: Stable reference content lives in the cached prefix. Pasting it into each message duplicates it and defeats caching.

questions.question: What should be true of the summary you carry forward after compaction?
options: It restates the system prompt so the instructions survive the reset
It keeps the full tool results, since those are the hardest to reconstruct
It is as short as possible, ideally one sentence describing the goal
It preserves task definition, decisions, exact values, and next steps
questions.explanation: Preserve state, drop chatter. The system prompt persists on its own, and a one-line goal loses the decisions and values later steps need.

questions.question: Which is a symptom of context overflow rather than a bad prompt?
options: Answers that are shorter than usual and skip the requested formatting
Late-conversation instructions ignored and earlier details contradicted
The model asks for information that was never provided in the conversation
Slower responses and higher cost per turn as the conversation grows
questions.explanation: Overflow shows as lost or contradicted details. Asking for missing information is a sign of too little context, and slower responses are a cost symptom, not a quality one.

questions.question: How do subagents relate to context budgets?
options: They share the coordinator's budget, so each subagent reduces what is left for the rest
They double the coordinator's window, since each subagent adds its own context to it
Each has its own budget, so heavy subtasks do not consume the coordinator's window
They have no budget of their own and rely on the coordinator to compact for them
questions.explanation: Separate budgets per subagent; only the returned summary lands in the coordinator's window.

questions.question: A nightly job classifies 50,000 support tickets into one of eight categories. Which architecture is right?
options: An orchestrator that spawns one classifier subagent per category and lets them vote on each ticket
An autonomous agent per ticket with tools to look up the customer's history before deciding
One agent with the full ticket export in context so it can spot category patterns
A batch workflow with a fixed prompt and schema-constrained output, plus a sampled human audit
questions.explanation: Fixed labels, huge volume, no branching: a batch workflow with constrained output and an audit sample. An agent per ticket adds cost and variance to a task with no open-ended path.

questions.question: Which question best decides whether a task needs an agent at all?
options: Can the steps be written down in advance, or does the path depend on what the model finds along the way?
Is the model capable enough to complete the task end to end without a human checking each intermediate step?
Is the budget large enough to absorb the extra tokens that an agent loop consumes?
Does the task involve tools, since tool use is what distinguishes an agent from a prompt?
questions.explanation: Agents are for open-ended paths; predictable steps are workflows or code. Workflows can use tools too, so tool use alone does not decide it.

questions.question: An agent's outputs are correct but users complain it 'never explains why'. What is the low-cost design fix?
options: Drop the structured output and return prose so the reasoning and the answer arrive together in one readable block
Enable extended thinking and return the thinking blocks to users as the explanation
Ask for a brief rationale alongside the structured result, kept separate from the machine-readable fields
Add a second model call that reads the result and writes an explanation for the user
questions.explanation: A separate rationale field gives users the why without breaking parsing. Thinking blocks are not written for end users, and a second call doubles cost for something the first call can produce.

questions.question: Two subagents produce partial reports and the coordinator must merge them into one document. What protects merge quality?
options: Let the coordinator read both partials in full and improvise a merged document
A fixed output schema for the partials so merging is deterministic, then one editing pass for coherence
Have each subagent read the other's draft before finishing so the two partials already agree on structure and content
Run the two subagents sequentially so the second one extends the first one's document
questions.explanation: Structured partials make the merge reliable; a final pass restores flow. Cross-reading drafts couples the workers and loses the parallelism that made the split worthwhile.

questions.question: Which is the right response when an agent's evaluator step disagrees with a human reviewer 30% of the time?
options: Trust the evaluator, since consistent model judgments beat a single reviewer's opinion
Calibrate the evaluator against the human labels, refine its criteria, and keep the human until agreement is high
Replace the evaluator with a second human reviewer, since a 30% disagreement rate shows model grading does not work here
Average the evaluator's score with the human's so neither judgment dominates the outcome
questions.explanation: Evaluators earn autonomy through measured agreement. Averaging hides the disagreement instead of resolving it, and abandoning the evaluator throws away a fixable component.

questions.question: A client wants the agent to run overnight unattended. Which capability must exist first?
options: A dashboard showing live progress so the team can check on it in the morning
A larger model, so the run makes fewer mistakes when nobody is there to correct it
Extended thinking on every turn so the agent reasons carefully without supervision
A hard stop on cost and turns plus alerting, so an unattended run cannot spiral
questions.explanation: Unattended means bounded and observable. A dashboard shows a spiral but does not stop it.

questions.question: What does 'fail closed' mean for an agent that hits an unexpected error?
options: Stop the action, record the state, and hand off to a person or a defined fallback
Restart the whole task from the beginning with a fresh context and the same inputs
Continue with the most likely interpretation and flag the guess in the final report
Retry the failing step with a different tool until one of them succeeds
questions.explanation: Fail closed protects against acting on bad state. Continuing on a guess is failing open, and blind retries can repeat a harmful action.

questions.question: An orchestrator-workers design is producing repeated work across workers. Likely cause?
options: Too few workers, so each one is covering more of the task than it can hold in context
The workers share one context window, so each one sees the others' progress and repeats it in its own output
Overlapping subtask briefs; the coordinator should partition the task so each worker's scope is disjoint
Missing evaluator step, so duplicate outputs are never caught before the merge
questions.explanation: Disjoint scopes prevent duplicate effort. Workers have separate contexts, and an evaluator would catch duplicates after the wasted work rather than prevent them.

questions.question: Which metric would you add to detect that an agent is 'succeeding' by giving up early?
options: Task completion checked against explicit acceptance criteria, not the model reporting done
Average tokens per task, since a run that gives up early uses noticeably fewer tokens than a full run
Tool calls per task, since an agent that stops early makes fewer calls than expected
Latency per task, since early exits finish faster than runs that do the whole job
questions.explanation: Verify completion against criteria, not self-report. Token, call, and latency counts are proxies that an efficient run and an early exit can share.

questions.question: A workflow needs a human to approve step three only when the amount exceeds a threshold. How do you model it?
options: Require approval on every run of step three, since a threshold check adds complexity
Instruct the model to decide when the amount seems high enough to ask a person
Have an evaluator model review step three's output and escalate whenever the amount looks risky
A conditional gate in the workflow that routes to a human queue when the condition holds
questions.explanation: Conditional gates are code, not model judgment. The threshold is known, so an evaluator's opinion adds variance where a comparison would do.

questions.question: Which practice keeps agent behavior reproducible enough to debug?
options: Setting temperature to zero, which makes each run identical for the same input and settings
Logging the exact prompts, tool inputs and outputs, and model settings per step
Using the largest model, since stronger models behave more predictably
Turning off prompt caching so each step is computed fresh from the raw prompt
questions.explanation: Reproduction needs the full record. Temperature zero does not guarantee identical outputs and does not tell you what the tools returned.

questions.question: A stakeholder asks why the agent needs a 'planning' step that costs extra tokens. Best answer?
options: The Agent SDK requires a planning turn before any tool call can be executed in a session
It makes the model look more deliberate, which builds stakeholder confidence in the output even when the plan is not followed
On multi-step tasks a plan cuts wasted tool calls and lets people review intent before actions, usually saving more than it costs
Plans are cached as part of the prompt prefix, so every later turn in the same run costs less per token than the first
questions.explanation: Plans cut thrash and enable review of intent before side effects. Nothing in the SDK requires a plan, and a plan in the conversation is not a cached prefix.

questions.question: A team wants Claude Code to follow its commit message convention every time. Which approach is reliable?
options: State the convention in CLAUDE.md with an example, and validate with a hook on commit
Tell Claude Code once at the start of the session and rely on it for the rest of the work
Delegate all commits to a subagent whose prompt contains the convention
Let Claude Code infer the convention from the existing git log before it commits
questions.explanation: Guidance plus enforcement. Inferring from the log works until the log has inconsistent history, and a chat instruction does not survive the session.

questions.question: Which is a good reason to use headless Claude Code inside a GitHub Action?
options: Interactive debugging of a failing build, where the developer talks to Claude in the CI logs
Exploring an unfamiliar codebase, since the runner has a clean checkout to learn from
Repeatable, reviewable automation such as summarizing a PR, with a fixed tool allow list
Pair programming on a feature branch, with the Action re-running after every push
questions.explanation: Headless suits repeatable, bounded jobs with a fixed allow list. Debugging and exploration need a person in the loop.

questions.question: A hook blocks a command but Claude Code keeps retrying variations. What is missing?
options: A stricter permission rule that denies the Bash tool entirely for the session
A second hook on the Stop event that ends the turn after the first block
A longer CLAUDE.md section repeating the rule the hook is enforcing
A clear block message that says what is disallowed and what to do instead
questions.explanation: Blocks need explanations to redirect behavior. Without a reason the model treats the block as a transient failure and tries again.

questions.question: What is the difference between a slash command and a skill in practice?
options: Slash commands need an MCP server behind them; skills run entirely from Markdown
A slash command is a reusable prompt you invoke; a skill packages a procedure with instructions and supporting files
Skills run in a separate subagent context by default; slash commands run inside the main session with its full history
Slash commands are built in; skills are only available through installed plugins
questions.explanation: Commands are prompts; skills are packaged procedures with their own files. Neither needs an MCP server, and both can be project-defined.

questions.question: Which permission stance fits a developer's laptop versus a shared CI runner?
options: The same rules in both, so behavior is predictable regardless of where it runs
Allow everything in CI since nobody is there to answer prompts, and deny most on the laptop
Interactive approvals on the laptop; a narrow pre-approved allow list with no prompts in CI
Deny all writes in both and let a human apply the changes Claude proposes
questions.explanation: Human present versus not present: approvals where someone can answer, a narrow allow list where nobody can. Allowing everything in CI is the opposite of what an unattended runner needs.

questions.question: Claude Code keeps reading the same large log file into context on every task. Fix?
options: A CLAUDE.md note to grep the log for specific patterns rather than reading it whole, or a tool that returns matches
Move the log's contents into the project CLAUDE.md so it is loaded once at startup and cached
Compact the session after each read so the earlier copies of the log leave the context before the next task starts
Increase the session's context budget so the full log fits without truncation each time
questions.explanation: Targeted retrieval over bulk reads. Compaction removes the copies after the cost has been paid, and putting the log in CLAUDE.md loads it on every session.

questions.question: Which statement about CLAUDE.md scope is correct?
options: One CLAUDE.md file per repository is allowed, and it must sit at the repository root
Files can live at the project root and in subdirectories, applying to work in those areas
CLAUDE.md is read only from the home directory, so project rules go in settings.json
Subdirectory CLAUDE.md files replace the root file entirely when Claude works in that area
questions.explanation: Scoped memory files per area, layered with the root file rather than replacing it.

questions.question: What should a team do before letting Claude Code run database migrations in a shared environment?
options: Grant the Claude Code process admin rights so the migration cannot fail on permissions
Disable hooks for the migration step so nothing interrupts a long-running command
Ask Claude Code to review the migration SQL itself for mistakes before running it against the database
Gate the migration command behind approval, run it against a staging copy first, and log the run
questions.explanation: Irreversible actions get gates and rehearsal. Self-review by the same model is weaker than a staging run and a human approval.

questions.question: A developer asks Claude Code to 'make the tests pass' and it edits the tests to always pass. What prevents this?
options: A longer timeout, so the model has time to fix the code rather than the tests
Removing the test files from the working tree during the task so only the source files are editable by the model
Running in plan mode so the model proposes edits but never applies them
Explicit instructions that tests define behavior and must not be weakened, plus review of test diffs
questions.explanation: State the constraint and review test changes. Plan mode stops all edits, including the fix that was asked for.

questions.question: When is a subagent overkill?
options: For a large investigation that would fill the main session with file contents
For a one-line lookup the main session can answer directly
For parallel research across several independent parts of the codebase
For isolating a noisy tool's output away from the main conversation
questions.explanation: Delegate for scope and isolation, not trivia. The other three are the cases subagents exist for.

questions.question: Which is the most reliable way to keep a chatbot on topic?
options: Lower the temperature so the model is less likely to wander from the topic
State the allowed scope and the exact behavior for out-of-scope requests, with an example refusal
Ask it in the system prompt to stay focused and professional throughout the conversation and avoid tangents
Limit max_tokens so long off-topic answers are cut off before they finish
questions.explanation: Define scope and the off-scope behavior. 'Stay focused' gives the model no definition of the boundary.

questions.question: A prompt uses the word 'summarize' but the stakeholder wants an executive brief with decisions and risks. What is the fix?
options: Add a persona of a chief of staff so the model understands who the reader is
Keep 'summarize' but add 'good' and 'executive' as qualifiers to signal the audience
Move to a larger model, since executive briefs need stronger reasoning than summaries
Replace the vague verb with the required sections and length, plus an example brief
questions.explanation: Name the sections and show an example. A persona hints at the reader but does not say what a brief must contain.

questions.question: What is the purpose of asking the model to plan before it writes a long document?
options: A structure to check and steer before tokens are spent on prose
Faster generation, since the model writes prose more quickly from an outline
Fewer examples needed, since the plan takes the place of a sample document
A longer output, since the plan and the document are both returned
questions.explanation: Plan first, then write against the plan. The gain is steerability, not speed.

questions.question: Which instruction helps most when the model must handle inputs in several languages?
options: Instruct the model to translate everything to English internally before answering
Tell the model it is multilingual and let it match whatever language the user writes in
State the expected input languages and the required output language explicitly
Provide one example conversation in each language the product supports
questions.explanation: Explicit language handling removes the guess about which language to answer in. Matching the user's language is one policy, but it needs to be stated, not assumed.

questions.question: You need consistent scoring of essays on a 1 to 5 rubric. What makes the prompt reliable?
options: A persona of a strict but fair teacher with twenty years of grading experience
A one-line instruction to score from 1 to 5, with temperature set to zero
Extended thinking so the model weighs each essay carefully before it commits to a score
The rubric spelled out per score level with an example essay at two or three levels
questions.explanation: Anchored rubrics with examples. Temperature zero makes the scores repeatable but not calibrated.

questions.question: The model returns Markdown when you need plain text for an SMS. Simplest fix?
options: Strip Markdown syntax in code after generation and accept the occasional artifact
Instruct plain text with no formatting, show an example, and validate before sending
Ask for the message twice and send whichever version contains fewer formatting characters
Switch to a smaller model, since smaller models use less formatting by default
questions.explanation: Specify, exemplify, validate. Stripping in code is a fallback, not a fix, and leaves artifacts in the message.

questions.question: Why keep examples in a prompt consistent in format with the required output?
options: Consistent examples compress better, which keeps the prompt within the cache limit
The API validates examples against the output schema and rejects mismatches
The model imitates the examples; inconsistent examples produce inconsistent output
Consistent examples let the model skip reasoning and copy the pattern directly
questions.explanation: Examples are templates the model imitates. The API does not validate examples, and caching does not depend on their format.

questions.question: What should you do when a system prompt and a user message conflict?
options: Design the system prompt to state precedence for the cases you care about, and test them
Remove the system prompt and put all instructions in the user turn so nothing can conflict
Rely on the default, since the system prompt is guaranteed to win any conflict
Raise the temperature so the model can weigh the two instructions more flexibly
questions.explanation: Make precedence explicit and tested. System prompts carry weight but are not a guarantee, so the cases that matter need stating.

questions.question: Which is a sign a prompt is over-specified?
options: Long rule lists the model ignores while output quality drops on normal inputs
Consistent output on the eval set but higher cost per call than the team expected
Cache hits fall because the system prompt changes with every rule added
The model asks clarifying questions on inputs the rules already cover
questions.explanation: Too many rules dilute the important ones. Higher cost with consistent output is a budget question, not a sign of over-specification.

questions.question: How do you test a prompt change without a full eval suite yet?
options: Ask the model to compare the old and new prompt and say which one it prefers
Change the prompt, the model, and the temperature together so any improvement shows clearly
A small fixed set of representative inputs, including edge cases, compared before and after
Ship the change to a small share of users and watch the support queue for complaints
questions.explanation: Small, fixed, representative. Changing several things at once means you cannot tell which change helped.

questions.question: A tool's parameters are named a, b, and c. Why does that hurt?
options: Single-letter names shrink the JSON payload, so this is a reasonable trade for speed
The schema will fail validation because JSON Schema requires property names of three or more characters
The model cannot infer meaning, so it guesses; descriptive names and descriptions fix it
It only matters if the tool has no description, since the description explains the parameters
questions.explanation: Names carry meaning to the model. A description helps, but the model reads the schema at call time and short names give it nothing.

questions.question: Which tool response is best for a 'list orders' call that matched 5,000 orders?
options: The first page with a total count and a cursor for more
All 5,000 orders, so the model has everything it needs in one call
An error telling the model to narrow the query before retrying
The total count only, with a note that details are available on request
questions.explanation: Paginate with a cursor and a total. Forcing a narrower query throws away a valid result, and a count alone gives the model nothing to work with.

questions.question: When should a tool call require confirmation in a Claude Code or Agent SDK setup?
options: Only for reads from production systems, since reads can expose sensitive data
When it writes, deletes, sends, or spends, until its accuracy is proven
For every call, since the cost of asking is small compared with any wrong action
Only when the model reports low confidence in the parameters it chose
questions.explanation: Side effects need gates until accuracy is measured. Confirming every call, including reads, makes the gate noise that people stop reading.

questions.question: What is the practical difference between exposing data as an MCP resource versus returning it from a tool call?
options: Resources are faster because the client caches them; tool results are fetched fresh every time
Resources are for structured data and tools are for text, so the choice follows the payload type
Resources require user approval before the client loads them; tool calls are executed by the model directly without a prompt
Resources are addressable read-only data the client loads when needed; tools perform actions and return results
questions.explanation: Resources are addressable read-only data the client loads on demand; tools perform actions and return their results. Neither is defined by payload type or caching.

questions.question: A remote MCP server should identify which agent is calling. Why?
options: Authorization, rate limits, and audit depend on knowing the caller
The stdio transport requires a caller id in every request frame
The server selects which model to use based on the calling agent
Identified callers get their tool lists cached, which speeds up discovery
questions.explanation: Identity underpins control. Model selection is the client's concern, and stdio is the transport a remote server does not use.

questions.question: An agent misuses a tool because its description was written for developers. What changes?
options: Add more parameters so the model has finer control over the tool's behavior
Keep the developer description and add a system prompt section explaining to the model how and when to use the tool
Rewrite it for the model: what it does, when to use it, when not to, parameter meanings, an example
Move the developer notes into the parameter descriptions where the model reads them
questions.explanation: Descriptions are model-facing, so rewrite the description itself. A system prompt section is further from the point of selection than the tool's own text.

questions.question: How should a tool report partial success, such as 8 of 10 records updated?
options: Return success, since most of the records were updated and the model can move on
Return failure so the model retries the whole batch until every record succeeds
Retry the failed records silently inside the tool and return success once they complete
Return a structured result listing what succeeded and what failed, with reasons
questions.explanation: Partial outcomes need detail. A blanket failure triggers a retry of the eight records that already succeeded.

questions.question: Which MCP transport suits a server that many users hit concurrently from a web app?
options: stdio, with one server process spawned per user session on the web host
Streamable HTTP, which supports remote, concurrent clients
A shared file system watched by the server for request files
WebSocket only, since HTTP cannot carry the server's notifications
questions.explanation: Remote, concurrent access is Streamable HTTP. stdio is for a local process owned by one client.

questions.question: Why keep tool schemas strict rather than accepting free-form strings?
options: Strict schemas are optional in the API, so this is a style preference rather than a requirement
Strict schemas let the model produce valid calls and let you validate before execution
Free-form strings are faster to generate, but strict schemas produce shorter code
Free-form strings are rejected by the Messages API, so strict schemas are required
questions.explanation: Validation before action. The API accepts string parameters; the point is that strict types catch bad calls before they run.

questions.question: An agent's context contains three copies of the same document from repeated tool calls. What is the fix?
options: Increase the context window so the duplicates fit alongside the rest of the task
Tell the model in the system prompt to ignore repeated documents and use the first copy
Add a compaction step after every tool call so older copies are summarized away
Deduplicate tool results and cache the document by identifier so it loads once
questions.explanation: Deduplicate and cache. Asking the model to ignore copies still pays for them, and compacting every call loses detail.

questions.question: What is the value of a 'scratchpad' or notes file for a long task?
options: It gives the model a place to write longer prompts for itself on the next turn
It lets tools run faster because their results are written to disk instead of context
Durable working memory outside the window, so progress survives compaction and restarts
It replaces the need for compaction, since the window stops growing once notes are kept
questions.explanation: External working memory that survives compaction. Notes do not stop the window from growing; they make compaction safe.

questions.question: Which order helps prompt caching for a multi-tenant assistant with shared instructions?
options: Shared instructions and tools first, tenant data after the breakpoint
Tenant data first so each tenant's cache is warm from the first token
Tenant data in the system prompt and shared instructions in the user turn
Alternate shared and tenant content so both are covered by the cache
questions.explanation: Shared prefix, tenant suffix. Tenant data first makes the prefix unique per tenant, so nothing is shared.

questions.question: A workflow step needs only two fields from a large upstream result. Best practice?
options: Pass the whole upstream result so the step has the full context available if it turns out to need more
Extract the two fields and pass only those, keeping an identifier to fetch more if needed
Summarize the upstream result in prose and pass the summary to the step
Merge the step into the upstream one so no data has to be passed between them
questions.explanation: Pass what the step needs plus a pointer. A prose summary may drop the exact values the step depends on.

questions.question: What does compaction risk if done carelessly?
options: Cache misses on the next turn, since the compacted conversation prefix no longer matches the cached one
Slower responses, since the model must re-read the summary before it can act
Dropping exact values, identifiers, or the current task definition that later steps need
More tool calls, since the model re-fetches everything the summary mentions
questions.explanation: Preserve precision-critical state. Cache misses are a real but minor cost next to losing the task definition.

questions.question: An agent must consult a policy document on every decision. Which approach balances cost and accuracy?
options: Keep it in the cached prefix, or retrieve the relevant section per decision
Summarize it once at session start and rely on the summary for every decision
Paste the full document into each user turn so it is always the freshest input
Load it through a tool call on each decision so it never occupies the prefix
questions.explanation: Cached prefix or targeted retrieval. A one-time summary loses the detail decisions depend on, and pasting per turn pays full price every time.

questions.question: Which is a symptom of too little context rather than too much?
options: Instructions from early in the conversation are contradicted late in the conversation
Responses slow down and cost per turn rises as the conversation grows longer
Cache misses increase because the shared prompt prefix changes from one turn to the next as history grows
The model asks for information it should have, or guesses at details that were never provided
questions.explanation: Missing inputs show as guessing or asking. Contradictions late in a conversation are the overflow symptom.

questions.question: How should you size retrieval chunks for a technical manual?
options: As large as the context window allows, so each retrieved chunk carries the full surrounding material of the manual with it
Large enough to hold one complete idea, like a procedure or section, and small enough to keep only relevant material in context
One sentence each, so retrieval can match the exact line the question is asking about
Whole chapters, since a manual's own structure already groups the related material together and keeps procedures whole
questions.explanation: Complete ideas, minimal noise. Single sentences lose the procedure they belong to, and chapters carry mostly irrelevant material.

questions.question: A coordinator agent's window is filling with subagent chatter. What is the structural fix?
options: Have subagents return only structured results and keep their transcripts out of the coordinator
Use fewer subagents so less of their output reaches the coordinator's window
Compact the coordinator's context after each subagent returns so the accumulated chatter is summarized away
Disable logging in the subagents so their tool output is not echoed back
questions.explanation: Return results, not transcripts. Compacting after the fact pays for the chatter first; fewer subagents reduces capability rather than fixing the leak.

questions.question: A complex workflow involves auditing a massive codebase across several distinct subsystems. How should a coordinator agent spawn the investigation subagents to minimize turn overhead?
options: Emit multiple subagent tool calls within a single assistant response turn
Invoke one subagent, wait for its ResultMessage, and then call the next subagent
Prompt the model to chain subagents sequentially via intermediate user confirmations
Run each subagent from separate CLI terminals using independent configuration directories

questions.question: A team needs to explore two divergent refactoring strategies from a shared codebase analysis without having either branch alter the baseline session history. Which mechanism should they use in the Agent SDK?
options: Execute manual compaction by sending /compact to split the conversation history
Define an Explore subagent inside the existing session options
Pass fork_session = True with resume set to the baseline session ID
Call query() passing the baseline session ID with continue_conversation = True

questions.question: A developer needs to detect when Claude invokes a subagent during an Agent SDK session across various version releases. Which block names should the code check for in tool_use events?
options: Subagent and Worker
TaskCreate and TaskUpdate
Delegate and Spawn
Agent and Task
questions.explanation: D. Agent and Task   Newer releases label the block Agent in tool_use events, while older releases used Task, and Task also still appears as a name in the tools list, so checking for both keeps detection working across versions. Subagent and Worker are not names the SDK actually uses for delegating work. TaskCreate and TaskUpdate belong to the built in task tracking tools rather than to subagent invocation. Delegate and Spawn are not valid tool names in the SDK at all.

questions.question: An agent session ended prematurely. The developer examines the resulting ResultMessage in the Claude Agent SDK. Which field is the primary indicator of how the loop terminated?
options: usage
subtype
result
stop_reason

questions.question: An architect wraps an internal read-only lookup as a custom tool in the Agent SDK, then finds that its calls always wait for one another even when Claude asks for several of them in the same turn. What makes the SDK willing to run those calls at the same time?
options: Setting readOnlyHint in the tool's annotations
Listing the tool in allowedTools so its calls are approved without a prompt
Raising max_turns so that more calls fit inside one round trip
Returning the lookup result as a single text block rather than structured content

questions.question: A team is deciding which parts of a feature build to hand to subagents and which to keep in the session they are working in. Which piece of work belongs in the main conversation?
options: A dependency audit whose command output runs to thousands of lines
Reworking one authentication path, where design, edit and tests each build on the last
A migration run under a tool list that permits writes in one directory only
A sweep of the test suite that comes back as a list of failing cases

questions.question: A payments agent must never call the refund tool before a lookup tool has returned a verified customer ID. Which Agent SDK arrangement blocks the refund call itself rather than asking the model to remember the order?
options: A PostToolUse hook on the lookup tool that appends the customer ID to the transcript
A paragraph in the system prompt telling Claude to call the lookup tool first
A PreToolUse hook matched to the refund tool that returns a deny decision and a reason
A SubagentStop hook that checks for a verified ID once delegated work finishes

questions.question: In an Agent SDK application, a custom tool handler queries a legacy backend and returns a text payload far larger than the default tool output limit. What happens to that result?
options: The output is written to disk and replaced with an error result citing the file path.
The SDK aborts the entire agent loop and raises an unrecoverable token exhaustion error.
The output text is silently truncated to fit the token cap and marked as successful.
The SDK automatically serializes the data into a base64 string within an image block.

questions.question: While inspecting the system init message at the start of an Agent SDK query, an engineer sees that a remote MCP server has a status of pending. What does that status indicate?
options: The server is reachable but has been switched off for this session by configuration
The server missed the startup deadline and was dropped from the session
The server returned a schema that capability discovery could not compile
The server has not connected yet, or its tool list came from the cache and it will connect on first use

questions.question: An architect building an agent with the Claude Agent SDK wants a built-in tool such as Bash kept out of Claude's context entirely, so the model never sees it and never tries to call it. How should that restriction be configured?
options: Add a scoped rule such as Bash(rm *) to the disallowed tools array
Omit the tool from the tools list, or name it bare in disallowed tools
Register the tool with an empty handler so its calls come back with nothing
List the tool in allowed tools and refuse it from the canUseTool callback

questions.question: During an agent loop, Claude issues a client tool call that omits a mandatory argument. The host application catches the error and returns a tool result with is_error set to true explaining the missing input. How does Claude typically react to this feedback?
options: Claude permanently disables the invoked tool for all subsequent interaction turns.
Claude automatically replaces the missing argument with null and resumes processing.
Claude retries two to three times with corrections before apologizing to the user.
Claude terminates the conversation session immediately and surfaces an unhandled exception.

questions.question: A platform engineer writes a codebase audit skill whose file discovery fills the invoking conversation with paths nobody reads again. Which frontmatter setting keeps that output out of the invoking conversation and returns only the findings?
options: Add isolation: subagent so that verbose tool output is suppressed while the audit runs
Add agent: background to detach the session for the duration of the audit
Add sandbox: isolated so that file reads happen in a separate process
Add context: fork, which hands the skill to a subagent of its own

questions.question: A developer asks Claude to write a helper that rounds currency amounts for invoices, and early attempts get the half-cent cases wrong in a different way each time. What should the developer hand Claude so the work gets checked without a person watching every attempt?
options: A detailed prose description summarizing general language coding conventions and syntax standards for the codebase
A directive to enter plan mode and generate an elaborate specification document
Concrete test cases with expected inputs and outputs that Claude can execute
A collection of negative code samples illustrating previous flawed implementations

questions.question: An architect wants Claude to help design a complex caching mechanism in an unfamiliar system before writing any implementation code. Which technique best surfaces unexpected edge cases, technical constraints, and trade-offs upfront?
options: Provide an initial implementation script and request a full line-by-line syntax review
Add a PreToolUse hook to intercept file edits and query external documentation endpoints
Enable plan mode with bypassPermissions so Claude can autonomously test alternative branches
Start with a minimal prompt and ask Claude to interview you using AskUserQuestion

questions.question: A developer notices that custom instructions added to their project memory system seem to be missing during a session. They want to check which memory files actually loaded into the active session rather than just listing candidate locations on disk. Which command should they run?
options: Run /doctor to view an active breakdown of every loaded project instruction and diagnostic health check
Run /context to inspect memory files loaded in the current session
Run /memory to view startup files that were loaded into context
Run /status to display the concatenated contents of all project memory files

questions.question: A root CLAUDE.md has to pull in a shared standards file kept elsewhere in the repository. The same document also mentions a second path in a sentence of prose, and that one must not be loaded. How should the two paths be written?
options: Write the import as @path/to/file and wrap the mentioned path in backticks
Write the import as @path/to/file and put a backslash in front of the mentioned path
Write the import as #include <path> and put the mentioned path in square brackets
Write both paths as markdown links and let the loader work out which one to expand

questions.question: A developer processes 50,000 records asynchronously with the Message Batches API and streams the resulting JSONL file. How should the application reliably correlate each output result with its original input record?
options: Read lines sequentially from the JSONL output because batch results preserve the submission order.
Match records using the unique custom_id value assigned to each request in the batch payload.
Correlate records by matching the generated message ID with the client-side array index.
Sort retrieved responses chronologically using the creation timestamp in the message payload.

questions.question: A request that puts strict schemas on several extraction tools comes back with a 400 saying the schema is too complex to compile. Which change to the schemas relieves that pressure?
options: Make parameters required, with a sensible default stated, rather than leaving them optional
Nest the optional properties inside sub-objects so the top level stays small
Replace plain string fields with unions that accept several formats
Raise the compilation timeout on the request so the schema has longer to compile

questions.question: An architect designs an agent pipeline where Claude must invoke intermediate lookup tools with guaranteed parameter schemas and subsequently return a strictly formatted JSON report to the client. How should these capabilities be configured in the API request?
options: Rely solely on conversational system prompt instructions without enabling grammar enforcement.
Apply strict tool use to tool schemas and extract final JSON from intermediate thinking tags.
Set output_config.format to enforce the JSON report and omit client tools from the request.
Combine strict tool use on the tool definitions with JSON outputs in output_config.format.

questions.question: An architect builds an automated intake router where incoming documents may match one of several business record schemas, each represented as a distinct tool. Which tool_choice setting ensures that Claude executes a tool call without forcing a specific named tool?
options: Setting tool_choice to auto to allow the model to choose between text and tools
Setting tool_choice to none to suppress direct conversational text responses
Setting tool_choice to any so that the model must invoke one of the available tools
Setting tool_choice to tool with a wildcard character matching all extraction schemas

questions.question: An architect is writing tests for a pipeline that submits work to the Message Batches API and wants to know when a malformed request will be caught. When is the params object of each request in a batch validated?
options: At submission, with the whole batch rejected if any request is malformed
During polling, with the batch halted at the first malformed request
In the client library, before the payload leaves the local process
While the batch runs, with validation errors returned once processing of the whole batch has ended

questions.question: In an automated agent loop, the system appends a clarifying text block into the user message alongside the tool_result block after a tool finishes running. What negative behavior can this message pattern cause in subsequent turns?
options: It causes Claude to produce empty responses with an end_turn stop reason.
It causes an immediate 400 error due to invalid tool result payload formatting.
It forces Claude to switch automatically to the model_context_window_exceeded stop reason.
It causes the API to bill input tokens at double the standard cache creation rate.

questions.question: An agent doing a long refactor is interrupted partway through, and the team resumes the session on the same machine the next morning. What does resuming give them back?
options: Files edited before the interruption are returned to the contents they had at the start
Background processes the agent had started are launched again
The conversation comes back, while the changes already written to disk are left where they are
The working tree is synchronized with the remote branch before work continues

questions.question: A support workflow with long transcripts keeps drifting toward the model's context window limit, and an architect proposes prompt caching as the remedy. What does caching actually change for this workflow?
options: Cached prefixes stop counting toward the window, so more turns fit before the limit
It lowers what repeated tokens cost while those tokens still fill the window
It compresses the earlier turns so that later messages take fewer tokens
It moves cached prefixes into client storage until the model asks for them

questions.question: A production agent sometimes gets a response whose stop reason is max_tokens and whose last tool_use block is cut off partway through. What should the application do with that response?
options: Reissue the request with more room for output so the tool call comes back complete
Return the partial block as a tool result and let Claude repair it on the next turn
Read what arrived and fill the missing arguments with defaults before running the tool
Read stop_details and retry the call on a fallback model
